what_its_for: Leucovorin is a form of folic acid (a B vitamin) used for two main purposes: (1) to protect your body from the harmful side effects of a cancer medicine called methotrexate — this is called 'leucovorin rescue'; and (2) to treat a condition called megaloblastic anemia (a type of anemia caused by low folic acid). It is also sometimes used along with a cancer drug called fluorouracil (5-FU) to help treat colorectal cancer.
how_to_take: Leucovorin comes as a tablet you swallow by mouth, or it can be given as an injection or IV (into a vein) in a clinic or hospital. If you are taking the tablets, swallow them whole with a full glass of water. You may take them with or without food. If you are receiving it by IV or injection, a nurse or doctor will give it to you. Always take it exactly as your doctor or pharmacist tells you — do not take more or less than prescribed.
dosing: Your dose depends on why you are taking leucovorin, your weight, kidney function, and the medicines you are taking alongside it. There is no single standard dose for all patients. Your doctor will calculate the right dose specifically for you. It may be taken once a day, every 6 hours, or on a specific schedule tied to your chemotherapy. Always follow your doctor's exact dosing schedule — timing is very important, especially when used with methotrexate.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — BUT only if it has not been too long since the scheduled time. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do NOT double up to make up for a missed dose. If you are on the 'leucovorin rescue' schedule after methotrexate, a missed or late dose can be dangerous. Call your doctor or nurse right away if you miss a dose in that situation.
storage: Store leucovorin tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C–25°C). Keep them away from light, heat, and moisture — do not store them in the bathroom. Keep the bottle tightly closed. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. If you have unused or expired tablets, ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of them.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking leucovorin with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) for certain infections, as this combination may make the antibiotic less effective. Do not take extra folic acid supplements or multivitamins containing folic acid without asking your doctor first, as this could interfere with your treatment. Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can reduce how well folic acid works in your body and may worsen side effects. Do not stop taking leucovorin or change your dose on your own.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: a severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing); seizures or convulsions; nausea or vomiting that prevents you from keeping the tablets down; signs of infection such as fever, chills, or sore throat; unusual bruising or bleeding; mouth sores; or any new or worsening symptoms. If you are on leucovorin rescue after methotrexate and feel very unwell, call your doctor immediately — do not wait.
when_it_works: When used to protect against methotrexate side effects, leucovorin works within hours of being taken as it quickly enters your cells and helps counteract the effects of methotrexate. For treating anemia caused by low folic acid, you may begin to feel more energy and improvement in symptoms within 1 to 2 weeks, though it may take a few weeks for your blood counts to fully return to normal. Your doctor will check your blood regularly to see how well it is working.
special_populations: Pregnant or breastfeeding women: Leucovorin is generally considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding since it is a form of folic acid, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children: Leucovorin is used in children as well; the dose will be adjusted based on the child's weight and condition. Older adults: Older adults may need closer monitoring, especially if they have kidney or liver problems. Kidney or liver disease: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely if your kidneys or liver are not working normally.
